intros.market: Five CAs control 88% of public certificate issuance, with ISRG at 32%, Google Trust Services at 21%, and DigiCert at 18%. The market's CR3 concentration stands at 71%, yielding an HHI of 1980, well above the 1500 threshold economists use to flag oligopolistic markets. Despite 88 trusted CAs in total, 74 operate in the long tail with minimal market share, creating a bifurcated ecosystem where systemic risk concentrates in a handful of operators.
intros.trust: 335 roots are trusted across the four major stores, but only 90 roots appear in all four simultaneously, and just 38 CA owners hold trust in Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft together. Microsoft uniquely trusts 142 roots absent from the other three stores, creating significant chain-building complexity for CAs serving enterprise Windows environments. Store disagreement forces CAs to maintain multiple certificate chains and complicates incident response, as a distrust action in one program may leave certificates valid in another.
intros.conc: The HHI of 1980 signals high market concentration, with the top three CAs issuing 71% of all certificates and the top five reaching 88%. ISRG and Google Trust Services alone account for 53% of the market, creating systemic dependency where operational failures at either CA would affect over half the web. This concentration amplifies the impact of the 1787 recorded incidents, as misissuance or governance failures at top-tier CAs ripple across a larger certificate population.
intros.tail: 74 CAs operate in the long tail with negligible issuance share yet hold full trust store inclusion, multiplying the attack surface without contributing proportional value. These tail CAs collectively represent 12% of market share but account for 55 of the 88 CAs subject to incident reporting, audit requirements, and root program oversight. Low transaction volume correlates with reduced operational maturity, as evidenced by incident data showing tail CAs contribute disproportionately to governance and validation failures.
intros.geo: CAs incorporated in the United States issue 93% of all certificates despite representing only 15 of 88 trusted CAs, while 44 European CAs contribute just 7% of issuance. Asia-Pacific CAs hold 17 trust positions but account for 0.09% of certificates, the same share as government-operated CAs globally. This geographic concentration mirrors market concentration, with US-domiciled ISRG, Google, DigiCert, and GoDaddy forming the core of the ecosystem.
intros.gov: 30 government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store positions but collectively issue only 0.09% of certificates, the same share as the entire Asia-Pacific commercial sector. These CAs present elevated jurisdiction risk due to direct state control, particularly the entities based in China, Russia, and other high-risk legal environments. Their minimal issuance volume does not eliminate systemic risk, as trust store inclusion grants these CAs the technical capability to issue for any domain on the internet.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions are classified as high legal risk for compelled disclosure or surveillance: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong, with India and Turkey at moderate risk. CAs incorporated in these regions face legal frameworks that permit or require cooperation with state intelligence agencies, creating a structural vulnerability separate from operational competence. This risk intersects with government CA presence, as 30 state-operated CAs navigate jurisdiction constraints that may conflict with root program independence requirements.
intros.ops: 1787 incidents have been recorded across 55 CAs, led by 680 misissuance events, 590 governance failures, and 383 revocation violations. CAs self-report only 32% of incidents, while external researchers discover 17%, automated tools find 15%, and root programs detect just 4%. Policy failures account for 262 incidents and disclosure failures for 164, suggesting systemic underreporting that inflates the true incident count beyond recorded figures.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture has migrated to RSA-4096 and ECDSA P-384 as dominant algorithms, with legacy SHA-1 and 1024-bit keys eliminated from active issuance chains. All 88 trusted CAs now operate roots meeting current algorithm and key size standards, though subordinate CA certificates issued from older roots continue to circulate. The BR Readiness tab tracks the separate challenge of certificate validity period compliance, where cryptographic compliance does not ensure operational readiness for upcoming lifetime reductions.
intros.distrust: 16 distrust events have occurred, with 14 involving compliance or operational failures and 10 attributed to patterns of repeated issues rather than isolated incidents. The posture distribution shows 7 cases of negligent noncompliance, 3 of willful circumvention, and 3 of demonstrated incompetence, indicating most distrusts stem from organizational failure rather than accident. The median runway of 1185 days from first incident to distrust suggests root programs exercise extensive forbearance before removal, creating long windows during which at-risk CAs continue issuing trusted certificates.
intros.policy: 35 active TLS CAs face cascading validity period reductions under SC-081, with 5 already compliant at 47 days, 9 ready for the 2029 deadline, but 3 still issuing above the 200-day threshold set for March 2026. The median validity period currently used is 62 days, indicating meaningful industry movement toward shorter lifetimes. This operational shift occurs against a compliance surface that has grown 121x since 2000 to 6657 total obligations, 76% mandatory, with zero clarifying ballots passed since 2022 despite the expanding requirement set.
intros.governance: Root program oversight has collapsed from 68-78% coverage in 2019 to 18% (Chrome), 10% (Mozilla), and 5% (Apple) in 2025, with Microsoft providing zero public engagement on the 223 incidents filed. Chrome has contributed substantive comments to 115 recent bugs from a corpus of 741 oversight threads, while Mozilla engaged substantively in 50 of 823 bugs. This declining coverage occurs as the incident rate remains high and distrust events average 1185 days from first issue to resolution, suggesting under-resourced programs struggle to maintain surveillance across 88 CAs.
intros.community: 56 organizations hold CA/B Forum membership, but only 21 participate actively in balloting, leaving 35 with zero contribution to policy development. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1, dominating individual participation, while Sectigo leads organizational engagement overall. This silent majority pattern concentrates policy influence among a few active CAs even as the regulatory surface has grown to 6657 obligations affecting all members.
intros.audit: Auditors detected just 30% of the 432 in-scope incidents that occurred during their audit periods, with 131 caught in letters and 301 missed, creating a systematic surveillance gap where clean opinions coexist with active compliance failures. 39 CAs show high transparency gaps between audit assertions and Bugzilla incident history, 6 have received qualified opinions, and only 13 auditors have adopted ETSI EN 319 403 v3.5 standards as of 2025. CAs self-report 64% of WebTrust issues and 70% of ETSI findings to auditors, suggesting both detection and disclosure failures contribute to the gap between audit assurance and operational reality.
